prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map captures the downward-tilted egocentric layout of a room where the seated camera wearer's knees, hands, and held notebook in the lower foreground are brightest at 0.3 to 0.7 metres (within arm's reach), resting above a low green-cloth stool about 0.8 to 1.2 metres away. To the right of the stool at roughly 1.2 to 1.8 metres lie a pair of blue shoes on the floor and a shoe rack against the right wall, while the wooden floor recedes to a doorway and mat at 2.0 to 3.0 metres in the upper background. Across frames 3 to 5, a second person enters through the upper-middle doorway and approaches forward and rightward toward the camera wearer, brightening from roughly 2.5 metres in frame 3 to 1.8 metres in frame 4 and 1.2 to 1.5 metres in frame 5, with their body facing generally toward the camera wearer's right side while their head and upper torso remain cropped above the top frame edge. The map makes it easier than RGB alone to gauge the continuous floor slope, the vertical elevation of the lifted notebook in frame 3, and the approaching person's exact distance relative to the stool and shoes. However, it is unreliable where per-frame auto-scaling causes the background floor and doorway in frame 3 to turn pitch black when the lifted book saturates the foreground brightness, and where fine details like the ruler, pencil, and individual shoes blur into the surrounding surfaces.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map outlines discrete foreground and background regions across the five frames, separating the camera wearer's hands and legs at 0.3 to 0.6 metres in the bottom foreground from the open book they hold (0.4 to 0.7 metres, within arm's reach) and the upper-right wall/doorway structure 1.5 to 2.5 metres away. In frames 1 to 4, the camera wearer's hands and forearms partially occlude the lower edge of the open book and the green stool beneath it, while in frame 5 the approaching person on the upper right is segmented at 1.2 to 1.5 metres, standing just behind and to the right of the stool with their upper body cropped out of view and their legs facing toward the foreground space between the stool and shoe rack. While the masks clearly isolate the boundary of the rotated book in frames 1 to 3 and the approaching person's silhouette in frame 5 against busy patterned textures, the semantic labels and consistency are highly unreliable. Specifically, the wooden door in the upper right is misclassified as a 'tv' in frames 1, 3, and 4, the shoe rack is mislabelled as a 'remote' in frame 1, the entire floor is merged into a 'dining table' mask in frame 2, and the green stool and book are conflated into a 'suitcase' in frame 3. Furthermore, the map completely misses the book and stool in frames 4 and 5, fails to detect the approaching person in frame 4, and fragments the camera wearer's own hands and legs into multiple separate 'person' instances.
descriptions.pose: The pose map renders only 2D magenta hand skeletons for the camera wearer's hands in the lower foreground at 0.3 to 0.6 metres (directly within arm's reach) against a black background, providing no scene layout or object geometry. In frame 1, both the left hand (lower left, palm down on the left page) and right hand (slightly higher and to the right, pinching the right page edge) are detected about 0.2 metres apart, whereas only the left hand is tracked in frames 2 and 4 as it holds the bottom-left corner of the tilted notebook. This skeletal wireframe reveals precise finger articulation and thumb opposition when gripping the notebook pages in frames 1, 2, and 4 that are partially obscured by motion blur and lighting glare in the RGB strip. However, the map is largely unreliable across the sequence because it completely misses the camera wearer's right hand in frames 2 through 5 (even when holding a ruler and pencil in frames 4 and 5) and loses both hands in frames 3 and 5 when they move near the bottom edge of the field of view. It also fails to generate any yellow body skeleton for either the camera wearer's visible legs in the bottom foreground or the second person approaching from 2.5 metres to 1.2 metres in the upper right of frames 3 to 5, whose head and gaze direction remain out of view above the frame.
